text:
Two, contamination. Test questions get published, published text gets crawled, and crawled text becomes training data. So a model that memorized the answers and one that can do the work report the same high score. That's what sank SWE-bench Verified in February: models could recite some of its fixes. The defense is a test it can't have seen: kept private, or newer than its training.

Three, selective reporting. A launch post picks its benchmarks, its rivals and its settings. Arc Prize ran GPT six Astra on Arc AGI three in two harnesses, the code wrapped around a model. In Arc's standard one, sixty-two point seven. In OpenAI's, which kept its hidden reasoning between moves, ninety-nine point nine, for less money. Same model, same test, same week. Only the first number compares with anyone else's.

Four, the deepest: construct mismatch. A benchmark measures the benchmark. SWE-bench predicts agentic coding, because the task looks like the job. It says almost nothing about reading your invoices. So a model that ranks third everywhere can still be the best one for you, and no leaderboard will say so. Ask four things of any row. All within three points? Could the model have seen it? Whose harness ran it? Does the task look like yours? If the last answer is no, there's one way to find out.
